strengths: The paper makes a genuinely novel contribution: the first information-theoretic treatment of layerwise PTQ optimality. The waterfilling lower bound (Prop. 3.1) and Theorem 3.3, which proves that entropy-coded GPTQ can have an arbitrarily large gap to the IT limit while WaterSIC is within a constant 0.255-bit gap, are clean, rigorous, and provide new understanding of a heavily studied problem.

The theoretical analysis is well-grounded in lattice quantization tools (flatness factors, Rényi entropy quantization results, Linder–Zamir continuity), and the proofs in Appendices A–B appear careful, including the elegant Lemma B.1 establishing independence of rounding error from the quantized coordinate.

The key algorithmic insight — unequal per-column grid spacings α_i = c/ℓ_ii mimicking waterfilling — is simple, well-motivated by theory, and empirically validated: column entropies indeed differ substantially (Fig. 5).

Empirical results are strong: SOTA WikiText-2 perplexity across four models (Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B, Qwen3-8B) at rates from 1 to 4 bits, with zero-shot benchmark comparisons in Appendix F and KL-divergence diagnostics.

Reproducibility effort is above average: full pseudocode (Algorithms 1–4), hyperparameter details, damping/mixing procedures, codec verification that entropy rates are achievable by Zstd/LZMA (Table 6), and component-wise ablations (Figs. 7–11). Limitations are honestly discussed (no end-to-end decompression benchmarking, moderate model sizes, Euclidean layerwise objective only).
weaknesses: A significant theory–practice gap: the 0.255-bit optimality guarantee holds for iid Gaussian weights and only asymptotically (a→∞, D→0, high-rate regime). The SOTA claims are made at 1–2 bits where the theory says nothing, so the theoretical guarantee and the empirical SOTA claim are only loosely coupled.

Rate comparison conventions are potentially misleading: WaterSIC reports entropy-based rates while several baselines (QTIP, NestQuant, AWQ, GPTVQ, QuIP#) report log-cardinality. Entropy rates for those baselines could be lower than their reported cardinality rates, so the claimed superiority over the strongest modern baselines (QTIP, NestQuant) is not established under a uniform rate metric.

The empirical gains conflate the core contribution with several techniques borrowed from prior work (Qronos-style activation drift correction, LMMSE shrinkage similar to QA-LDLQ, residual stream compensation, attention weighting). There is no head-to-head comparison of e.g. Huffman-GPTQ vs PlainWaterSIC with the same additional machinery, so the specific benefit attributable to waterfilling rate allocation in real LLMs is hard to isolate.

Reproducibility concerns: the pipeline involves substantial model-specific hand-tuning (manually zeroing specific outlier rows of Qwen3-8B layers 6 and 16, per-layer golden-section searches, dead-feature erasure with tuned thresholds), and no code release is stated. This complexity, plus the acknowledged absence of decompression-throughput benchmarking, limits practical applicability assessment — variable-length entropy-coded weights raise deployment questions that are deferred.

Evaluation breadth is modest: primarily WikiText-2 perplexity at context 2048 on models up to 8B; Llama-3-70B and comparisons to AQLM/PV-Tuning are deferred to future work, and several strong baselines (YAQA, PV-tuning) are excluded with the justification that evaluations are unavailable.

Presentation has notable editorial sloppiness (e.g., 'arithmetic mean-geometric Mean (AMGM)', 'igone', 'amout', inconsistent notation around (40)-(51) where α plays dual roles), which occasionally impedes reading of the otherwise careful proofs.

strengths: The paper offers the first genuine information-theoretic treatment of layerwise LLM PTQ, formalizing weight-only quantization as a rate-distortion problem (Section 3, Prop. 3.1) and deriving a rigorous asymptotic characterization of entropy-coded GPTQ (HPTQ) vs. the proposed per-column spacing scheme, with proofs using lattice flatness factors (Appendix B).

The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: identifying GPTQ's uniform spacing (A = αI) as suboptimal via the AM-GM inequality and replacing it with column spacings αi = c/|ℓii|, i.e., a waterfilling-style rate allocation, with a provable asymptotic rate gap of only 0.255 bits to the waterfilling converse.

The empirical evaluation is broad for the field: WikiText-2 perplexity across four models (Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B, Qwen3-8B) and rates from 1 to 4 bits (Tables 1, 2, 7, 8), plus zero-shot accuracy (Tables 9, 10) and extensive ablation/diagnostic material in Appendix E.
The limitations section is candid, explicitly flagging the lack of (de)compression throughput benchmarks, the layerwise/MSE objective restriction, and the model scale ceiling.
weaknesses: A central theory–practice gap: the 0.255-bit optimality claim (Theorem 3.3) holds only (i) under an iid Gaussian weight model, (ii) in the joint limit a → ∞ and D → 0 (a high-rate asymptotic), and (iii) relative to a relaxed converse that allows ΣX-dependent decoding. The practically interesting regime for this paper's own results is 1–2 bits, where the high-rate analysis and Gaussianity are both questionable, yet the abstract and title advertise 'near optimal' unconditionally.

The headline SOTA claims rest on a rate-accounting asymmetry that is under-justified: WaterSIC and Huffman-GPTQ report entropy rates while QTIP, NestQuant, AWQ, etc. report log-cardinality (Figs. 1–2, Tables 1, 7, 8). Entropy coding of baseline outputs (or at least an analysis of how much rate QTIP/NestQuant could shed under entropy coding) is not provided, so several 'best in group' comparisons at matched bitwidth are not apples-to-apples. Margins like 2.00 vs. 2.02 bits (Table 1) are within the noise of this accounting choice.

The full pipeline conflates the theoretically motivated core with a large stack of heuristics: Qronos-style drift correction, residual stream compensation, attention-weighted calibration, per-layer golden-section search over two mixing parameters, diagonal rescalers, dead-feature erasure, and even zeroing specific outlier weight rows of the unquantized Qwen3-8B model (Appendix D). The claim that 'gains are additive with more sophisticated base quantizers' is asserted, not demonstrated, and the per-layer hyperparameter search on calibration data is a level of tuning not matched by the compared baselines.

Variable-length entropy-coded weights are not a drop-in replacement for fixed-rate formats: inference-time (de)compression cost, random access to weights, and kernel integration are unaddressed (admitted in limitations), which materially weakens the practical significance of 'new SOTA' at a given average bitrate.

Zero-shot results are mixed and selectively presented: Table 9 shows Huffman-GPTQ winning several benchmarks at 1.5 and 2.0 bits, and Table 10 shows GPTQ/HRTN leading on several tasks at 4.125 bits, which tempers the 'establishes new SOTA' framing drawn primarily from perplexity.

No code release or artifact link is mentioned; given the intricate pipeline (binary search over c per layer with row subsampling, sequential budget reallocation, golden-section searches, model-specific outlier surgery), independent reproducibility is a serious concern.

Presentation quality is below the bar: numerous typos and errors ('bulding', 'aggreessive', 'amout', 'calibratron', 'be nchmarks', 'WaterSIC's is', 'the the'), loose notation (D* used both for the IT limit and for scheme outputs on p. 4), and results-critical details (rate conventions, baseline provenance) relegated to figure captions and footnotes.

strengths: The paper offers the first serious information-theoretic treatment of layerwise weight-only quantization: it derives a waterfilling converse (Prop. 3.1), identifies the precise structure of Huffman-GPTQ's gap to the IT limit (Theorem 3.3), and shows the proposed per-column spacing α_i = c/ℓ_ii closes the gap to a constant 0.255-bit offset (2πe/12). The proofs in Appendices A–B (lattice flatness factors, Rényi's rounding-entropy result, Linder–Zamir continuity) appear careful and non-trivial.

The core algorithmic insight is simple and elegant: GPTQ/ZSIC with uniform spacing A = αI is provably suboptimal, and a diagonal spacing matrix matched to the Cholesky diagonal implements a waterfilling-like rate allocation. The insight is cleanly isolated: the base quantizer is plain rounding plus entropy coding, no scaling or fine-tuning, so the reported gains are attributable to the new idea.

Empirical results are strong and extensive: consistent perplexity-rate improvements over Huffman-GPTQ, QTIP, NestQuant, QuIP#, GPTVQ, and AWQ on four models (Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B, Qwen3-8B) from 1 to 4 bits, plus zero-shot benchmark comparisons (Tables 9–10), KL-divergence analysis, per-component ablations (Figs. 7–11), and verification that entropy estimates translate into actual Zstd/LZMA compression (Table 6).

The limitations section is candid and specific (layerwise MSE objective only, no end-to-end (de)compression throughput benchmark, mid-sized models only), and the appendix documents practical pathologies (dead features, Qwen3-8B outlier rows, drift-correction instability at depth) with unusual honesty.

Rotation invariance of WaterSIC (performance depends only on |Σ_X|), and the demonstration that GPTQ's performance degrades under random rotations, is a practically relevant diagnostic that follows naturally from the theory.
weaknesses: The headline 'near-optimal' claim is conditional on strong assumptions that are acknowledged but soften the result: rows of W modeled as iid Gaussian, high-rate/low-distortion asymptotics (α→0, D→0, a→∞), and synthetic Gaussian weights for the 0.255-bit gap. At the practically relevant 1–2 bit rates where the empirical gains are largest, the high-rate analysis does not strictly apply, and the paper provides no quantitative bridge (e.g., simulations comparing actual WaterSIC rate-distortion curves to R_WF at fixed finite rates).

Practical deployability of variable-rate entropy-coded weights is a major unresolved issue. Weight tensors in LLM inference are accessed at arbitrary, data-dependent locations during matrix multiplication; variable-length codes complicate or preclude standard GEMM kernels and random access. The paper reports entropy rates as bitwidth but does not benchmark decode throughput or hardware interaction (explicitly listed as a limitation), which weakens the significance of the SOTA claim relative to fixed-rate methods like QTIP/NestQuant that are directly deployable.

Some comparisons are at slightly unequal footing: Qwen3-8B results rely on zeroing specific outlier rows/columns in the unquantized model and dead-feature erasure — preprocessing the base model in ways the baselines did not — although the authors do verify the PPL impact is below 0.01. Per-layer golden-section searches over (ε_qr, ε_aw) with full re-quantization at each evaluation also add substantial, unreported computational cost.

The manuscript does not mention a code release, which limits reproducibility of a method with many interacting components (binary search over c, sampled-row rate calibration, alternating rescaler optimization, per-layer mixing-parameter search).

Relative to the very recent Chen et al. (2025) result that GPTQ = Babai/ZSIC with A = αI, the incremental conceptual step (choosing A = diag(c/ℓ_ii)) is small, though the provable 0.255-bit characterization is genuinely new. There are also minor presentation defects (typos such as 'amout', 'be nchmarks', 'bulding'; 'AMGM' vs 'AM–GM'; some dense equation chains in Sec. 3.2).

strengths: Novel and meaningful theoretical contribution: the paper provides the first information-theoretic analysis of layerwise weight-only quantization, rigorously proving (Theorem 3.3, Appendices A-B) that standard entropy-coded GPTQ can have an arbitrarily large rate gap to the waterfilling IT limit (via the AMGM term in (13)), while the proposed WaterSIC closes this gap to at most 0.255 bits — the provable suboptimality of the scalar integer lattice. The reduction to successive interference cancellation and the choice αi ∝ c/ℓii (predictive/conditional innovation scaling) is an elegant and well-motivated instantiation of the Zamir et al. (2006) prediction-based achievability scheme.

The proofs are technically careful: Lemma 3.2 (decision regions), the flatness-factor argument for near-uniformity of quantization error, and the uniform Rényi entropy continuity argument are plausible and self-contained. The paper also honestly separates the exact asymptotic statements (a→∞, D→0) from the approximate finite-rate regime.

Strong, broad empirical validation: state-of-the-art perplexity across 1–4 bits on Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3-70B, and Qwen3-8B, including comparisons to QTIP, QuIP#, AQLM, PV-Tuning, NestQuant, GPTVQ, AWQ, and Huffman-GPTQ. Gains hold even for the non-finetuned WaterSIC against entropy-coded baselines, isolating the contribution of rate allocation.

Unusually thorough diagnostics: verification that reported entropies match achievable compression by Zstd/LZMA (Table 6), empirical Gaussianity checks of weights via KS statistics (Fig. 11), ablations of every pipeline component (residual compensation, drift correction, attention weighting, adaptive mixing), calibration/finetuning dataset sensitivity, and calibration context-length sensitivity. Hyperparameters are documented in detail and code is released, supporting reproducibility.

Honest limitations section: acknowledges the layerwise MSE objective vs. end-to-end KL (YAQA), lack of (de)compression throughput benchmarking, and moderate model sizes — these do not overstate the contribution.

Significant practical relevance: establishing that the Pareto frontier of bits-per-parameter may be lower than previously believed, and showing watermark-style entropy coding is compatible with hardware trends (Blackwell support), connects the work to active questions (memorization/capacity bounds).
weaknesses: The 'near-optimality' claim is conditional on the iid Gaussian weight model. The empirical Gaussianity check shows systematic departures exactly where they matter (wq, wk tails are heavier and Laplace fits are sometimes preferred), so the 0.255-bit gap to the IT limit is not guaranteed for real LLMs; the theoretical optimality result and the empirical SOTA claims are therefore somewhat loosely coupled, and the paper could better quantify the rate gap achieved on actual models.

Rate comparability across baselines is imperfect: WaterSIC reports rates via entropy while several baselines (QTIP, AWQ, GPTVQ, QuIP#) report log-cardinality, and fixed-rate methods cannot exploit variable-length coding. Although the paper follows prior conventions and also compares against entropy-coded Huffman-GPTQ, matched-rate comparisons against the strongest vector/trellis quantizers at exactly the same bit budget are not fully clean.

The full algorithm involves a substantial stack of heuristics beyond the core idea (LMMSE shrinkage, drift correction with per-layer golden-section search over two mixing parameters, attention-weighted calibration, dead-feature erasure, model-specific manual interventions such as zeroing specific outlier rows of Qwen3-8B, secant rate-matching). The empirical gains are hard to attribute cleanly to the theoretical rate-allocation innovation alone, and per-layer search adds quantization-time cost that is not benchmarked.

Practical deployment concerns are acknowledged but not resolved: entropy-coded, variable-length integer codes do not directly support fast standard GEMM kernels, and no decompression throughput or end-to-end inference latency is reported. As presented, the method demonstrates a better rate-distortion frontier rather than a deployable quantization format.

At the very low-bit end against the strongest finetuned baselines (e.g., PV-Tuning at 2 bits), WaterSIC trails on C4 perplexity (Table 13), and some zero-shot results are mixed (e.g., ARC-C below Huffman-GPTQ at 1.5 bits in Table 17), so the 'new SOTA in many categories' claim, while mostly supported, is not uniform across every setting.

The distortion model uses a single token-position-averaged covariance; the attention-weighting and adaptive-mixing fixes (Sections 4, Appendix C) implicitly acknowledge that this objective is misspecified for attention layers, indicating the clean IT formulation does not fully cover the actual models without the added corrections.

strengths: First information-theoretic treatment of layerwise weight-only quantization: the paper formalizes the rate-distortion problem, derives a waterfilling lower bound (Prop. 3.1), proves GPTQ/Huffman-GPTQ can have an unbounded gap to that bound, and shows a per-column spacing choice α_i = c/ℓ_ii closes the gap to a constant 0.255 bit (Thm 3.3), with proofs in the appendix (flatness factor arguments, Rényi entropy continuity). This is a genuinely new understanding of why GPTQ-style methods work and when they fail.

The core idea — unequal per-column rates via entropy coding, implicitly implementing waterfilling without PCA rotations — is elegant and well-motivated, and the paper correctly connects it to classical results (Zamir et al. 2006 prediction-based achievability; lattice quantization suboptimality).

Substantial empirical evaluation: 5 models (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-70B) across 1–4+ bits, with perplexity on two corpora, KL divergence, zero-shot benchmark suites, comparisons to many baselines (Huffman-GPTQ, QTIP, QuIP#, NestQuant, AWQ, GPTVQ, PV-Tuning), and ablations/diagnostics (per-component MSE plots, column-entropy distributions, weight Gaussianity KS tests, actual Zstd/LZMA compression sanity checks).

Reproducibility appears adequate: code is released, Algorithms 3–4 and hyperparameter details (damping, golden-section search, FT schedule) are documented, and limitations are honestly discussed (layerwise Euclidean objective only, no throughput benchmarking, model scale).
weaknesses: A gap between the theory and the deployed algorithm: Theorem 3.3 holds in the high-rate/low-distortion limit (α→0, D→0), whereas all practical results are at 1–4 bits where the asymptotic regime does not apply. The headline 'IT (near) optimal' framing therefore overstates what is proven for the rates that matter; the paper does not quantify the gap at practical rates.

The experimental SOTA comes from a long pipeline of heuristics layered on PlainWaterSIC (LMMSE shrinkage, Qronos drift correction, residual-stream compensation, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing via per-layer golden-section search, dead-feature erasure, manual zeroing of specific outlier rows on Qwen3-8B, and post-hoc finetuning). The theory motivates only the per-column spacing; the causal attribution of gains to the IT insight vs. engineering is muddied, and ablations are relegated to the appendix and cover only part of the stack.

Deployment practicality of variable-length entropy-coded weights is not established: inference on conventional hardware needs fixed-offset access or decompression, and the authors concede that end-to-end (de)compression throughput and kernel interaction were not benchmarked. Since the practical value of PTQ hinges on inference efficiency, this is a significant limitation for significance even though it is acknowledged.

Rate comparisons are partly asymmetric: WaterSIC reports rates via empirical entropy while several baselines report log-cardinality; the paper flags this convention difference, but the SOTA claims in figures/tables depend on it, and some baselines (QTIP, QuIP#) cannot be trivially converted to entropy-coded rates for a matched comparison.

The iid Gaussian weight model, while empirically supported for most matrix types, is weakest exactly for wq/wk (the authors' own KS analysis shows Laplace fits sometimes better and heaviest tails), which are also the layers where their extra attention-weighting/mixing machinery is needed — the theory's coverage of the hardest cases is least secure.

Presentation is rough for a main-track submission: numerous typos and editorial errors (e.g., 'Guassianity', 'amout', 'calibratrion', 'gquantization', inconsistent γ/γ̃ and c/α notation between Sections 3–4 and Algorithm 3), and Figure 1's caption/axis conventions require careful decoding.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated theoretical contribution: the paper provides the first information-theoretic analysis of layerwise weight-only quantization, connecting GPTQ to lattice quantization (ZSIC / Babai-style rounding) and deriving a clean rate-gap result (Theorem 3.3) showing GPTQ's gap to the waterfilling lower bound is governed by an AM-GM term that can be arbitrarily large, while the proposed per-column rate allocation (αi = c/ℓii, i.e., waterfilling via Cholesky diagonals) closes this to the universal 0.255-bit lattice penalty.

The core insight — that all prior methods fix a uniform rate across columns, contradicting classical waterfilling rate allocation — is simple, principled, and clearly the right conceptual contribution; it is also practically consequential.

Proofs in the appendices are substantive and largely self-contained: Lemma 3.2's decision-region argument, Lemma B.1's independence/boundedness argument, and the use of lattice flatness factors plus Rényi's high-resolution entropy result are appropriate tools used correctly.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: five models (Llama-3.2-1B/3-8B/2-7B/3-70B, Qwen3-8B), rates from 1 to 4+ bits, WikiText-2 and C4 perplexity, KL divergence, and zero-shot benchmark suites; comparisons include QTIP, NestQuant, QuIP#, GPTVQ, AWQ, Huffman-GPTQ, PV-Tuning, and DB-LLM at 2 bits.

Honest and thorough ablations: per-layer relative MSE ablations for each pipeline component (residual compensation, Qronos drift correction, attention weighting, adaptive mixing), a study of calibration/finetuning corpus effects, empirical verification of the Gaussian weight assumption via KS tests, and verification that entropy rates are achievable with real codecs (Zstd/LZMA, Table 6).

Limitations are candidly discussed (layerwise Euclidean objective, no hardware throughput benchmarking, model-size range), and code is stated to be released with detailed hyperparameters (Appendix D).
weaknesses: A substantial gap exists between the clean theory (PlainWaterSIC) and the deployed algorithm: the full WaterSIC piles on many empirical heuristics (LMMSE shrinkage, residual stream correction, Qronos drift correction with adaptive εqr/εaw mixing, attention-weighted calibration, dead-feature erasure, diagonal rescalers, secant-based rate matching, per-layer golden-section searches). The 0.255-bit near-optimality claim technically applies only to PlainWaterSIC in the a→∞, D→0, iid Gaussian setting; it does not certify near-optimality of the practical pipeline, and the ablations are reported as per-layer MSE rather than end-to-end perplexity deltas.

The theoretical guarantees are high-rate/asymptotic, whereas the practically interesting regime (1–2 bits) is far from D→0; the paper does not quantify how the gap behaves at low rates, so the 'near optimal' framing is stronger than what is proven for the operating regime.

Baseline rate comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: entropy-coded methods (WaterSIC, Huffman-GPTQ) report rates via entropy while QTIP/NestQuant/AWQ use log-cardinality, and the paper only loosely follows 'conventions of the respective references.' Entropy rates systematically understate practical bitstreams (their own Table 6 shows Zstd/LZMA land ~0.05–0.15 bpp above entropy), which inflates the apparent SOTA margin; also no decode-throughput comparison is given, so the practical deployability of variable-rate entropy coding relative to fixed-rate lattices remains open.

Some SOTA claims conflate configurations: WaterSIC-FT (with 4-epoch distillation finetuning) is compared against non-finetuned baselines in several tables (e.g., Table 1, Table 14), and Table 18 shows WaterSIC-FT sometimes underperforming WaterSIC on individual benchmarks, suggesting fragility; Table 10/13 show PV-Tuning still ahead on some metrics at matched bitwidth.

Presentation has noticeable rough edges (typos: 'bulding', 'ane entropy coding', 'gquantization', 'amout', 'tr means'; some cramped figures such as Figs. 4, 6–10 whose axes are hard to read; Algorithm 3's γk update vs. γi notation inconsistency), which slightly impedes reproducibility of the exact pipeline despite the released code.

Calibration and (default) finetuning are performed on the WikiText-2 train split with evaluation on the WikiText-2 test split — same-domain calibration that can flatter PPL numbers, partially addressed by the C4/RedPajama experiments but not the default headline results.
